learningObjective: Explain GSPMD's sharding-propagation design: how user annotations become a fully sharded graph.

canonicalClaims.claim: GSPMD's sharding propagation takes a partially-annotated computation graph and infers sharding specs for unannotated tensors by pushing constraints through operators (e.g. an elementwise op forces its inputs and outputs to share sharding; a matmul propagates according to which contracting/batch/non-contracting axes are sharded), inserting reshard collectives at boundaries where required and produced sharding disagree.
conditions: The graph contains at least one user sharding hint.
nonImplications: Does not imply propagation is unique — for many graphs several consistent sharding assignments exist; GSPMD uses heuristics/cost to choose.
Does not imply the user must annotate every tensor; propagation is designed precisely to avoid that.

misconceptions.claim: GSPMD is a pure runtime system: it reads sharding hints at run time and dispatches per-op parallel implementations without any compile-time transformation.
misconceptions.whyWrong: GSPMD is a compile-time partitioning pass in XLA that rewrites the HLO graph before execution.

misconceptions.claim: GSPMD requires every tensor to carry a user-specified sharding annotation; missing annotations are a compile error.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Propagation exists precisely because the user only annotates a few key tensors; the compiler fills in the rest.

misconceptions.claim: GSPMD propagates sharding but never inserts collectives; users must place All* ops manually where needed.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Reshard collectives are inserted automatically by the partitioner wherever adjacent ops disagree on required sharding.
